personas.why: The jumping dot makes the bug visible without code. I'd send the 14-versus-11 sequence to a teammate; the later form verdict interests me less.
I want to know where the three extra reps came from. Once the count gets back to 11, the question I stayed for is answered.
The impossible squat gets my attention, and the freeze makes me look for the fault. Then HOW IT WORKS appears when I'm still waiting to see the supposed squat.
I can follow the knee wave. I just wanted to see what the camera mistook for a squat, and by ten seconds I'm still waiting.
The pencil lifting when the knee disappears is a lovely way to explain missing evidence. That feels like a complete lesson; I don't need a second one on form.
Seeing a real clip turn into joints, then a wave, then a wrong count makes this feel like a project I could try. I'd save the build map.
The raw, reference and cleaned counts are easy to compare. I'm still interested in the personal baseline, but the judge diagram interrupts just when I want the result.
The count has a number I can check. Calling another set 'my best' doesn't yet tell me why a difference from it warrants stopping.
I'd save the hidden-knee example for explaining why a system should sometimes give no answer. The clip and the blank trace make that point better than a slide would.
The marked rep makes me curious about the decision. When the reel starts deriving a knee wave instead, it feels like a long route back to that decision.
The misplaced tick and the jump are the moment I'd replay. After the clean 11 lands, the form question feels like the hook for another reel.
The 0.2-second slip is memorable, but my eye went to the verdict stamp. By the section card I'm unsure which reveal I'm waiting for.
The raw frame beside the bad reading is the bit I'd send to another dev. It shows what failed rather than just putting a skeleton over gym footage.
I'd stay for the trace and comment to ask which detections were rejected. Getting 11 in total is encouraging, but doesn't show it found the right 11.
I want to compare the two actual reps, so I'll wait for the ghost overlay. I'd discuss the visible difference with a client, not treat the AI's stamp as a coaching cue.
I stopped to see a ridiculously fast squat. Switching to a different set before showing the counting mistake loses me.
